subject: treasureChest
pitch: A pirate's treasure chest with its lid thrown open. Weathered dark wood planks bound with rusty iron straps and studs, a heavy padlock hanging loose, and spilling out of it: gold coins, a pearl necklace, a jewelled goblet and a few red and green gems. A small skull-and-crossbones is carved on the front.
reasoning:
I'm planning the TypeScript module structure, setting up a root joint and a hinged lid joint at the back top edge, with chest dimensions around 0.9m wide, 0.55m deep, 0.45m body height, and a lid that opens to roughly 110 degrees.

I'm working out the hinge rotation math to make the lid swing up and back from its closed position, settling on a -110 degree rotation about the X axis so the lid leans backward when open, and now sketching the lid geometry as a half-cylinder shape using a partial cylinder rotated onto the x-axis.

Since the half cylinder leaves the flat bottom face open, I need a hidden backing: I'll add a thin interior plank colored deep red velvet for the lid's underside, then build the chest body from separate wall boxes (front, back, left, right, bottom) so the top stays open, and fill it with a flattened pile of gold coins.

Now I'm sizing the body (width, depth, height, wall thickness) and constructing each wall from stacked plank boxes with slightly varying colors and offsets for a weathered look, looping through front, back, and side walls. I'm also planning iron straps as vertical bands on the front and matching curved straps wrapping over the lid's half-cylinder shape.

Adding strap rings, corner brackets, and stud details to the hardware, plus a bottom iron band for reinforcement. I'm also designing a lock assembly—an iron plate with a keyhole on the body front, and a hanging padlock attached by a loop near the hasp.

I'll place a carved skull plaque above the lock, centered at x=0, y≈0.31, with the staple and hanging padlock below around y=0.17 down to y=0.1. For the skull itself, rather than relying on an SVG texture (which won't rasterize reliably), I'll build it from a flattened, squashed sphere in a darker wood tone to suggest a carved inset.

For readability I'm switching the skull's color to a lighter burnt-tan/scrimshaw tone instead of dark-on-dark, with black spheres for eye sockets and crossbones made from thin rotated boxes with end knobs. I'm positioning the plank detailing at a slightly raised z-depth in front of the chest's outer wall, and sketching the gold treasure pile as a flattened sphere sized to fit within the interior cavity dimensions.

Now I'm scattering coin cylinders across the gold mound and spilling some over the front rim onto the floor using randomized positions and tilts—roughly 60 coins on the mound and 40 in the spill, with a few draping over the rim and a small heap forming where they land in front of the chest.

For a pearl necklace, I'm defining a draping curve from inside the chest, over the rim, down the front wall, and pooling onto the floor, using a series of control points to form a catmull-rom path that spheres will follow for individual pearls.

Continuing with more spacing math around the strap thickness so the pearls avoid clipping into it, then planning to sample pearl spheres along the path using an SDK catmull helper at regular intervals, with a small gold clasp capping the end. Now I'm considering where to place the goblet—whether standing upright on the gold pile or toppled over on the floor.

I'll give the goblet a gold tint with a slight tilt, and scatter gem accents—ruby and emerald icosahedrons/octahedrons—on the mound and goblet, plus spilled coins positioned randomly across the mound's ellipsoid surface.

I'm checking that part counts (coins, studs, pearls, planks) stay well under 1000 and triangle counts stay low enough for performance, while limiting materials to a reasonable palette of flat colors including wood variations.

I'm weighing whether to add grain paint texture to the lid for visual interest versus keeping everything flat-colored to reduce risk, since the bake happens at bind-pose coordinates during mesh creation. I'll lean toward flat colors for the body and planks to keep things simple and reliable.

Setting up joints next: root at origin, a hinge joint for the lid with rotation around the local X axis for opening, and a padlock joint hanging from the staple with a slight tilt and an open shackle rendered as a partial torus.

I'm defining helper functions for parts (box and generic geo) that always specify an explicit bone to avoid defaulting to the nearest joint, then laying out the lid pieces as a half-cylinder spanning the hinge depth, centered at the hinge's y position.

Since the transform composes as translate-rotate-scale, scale happens in the geometry's local axes before rotation — so to get the world-space thinness I need after rotating the cylinder 90° about z, I scale local x by 0.75 instead of y.

For the straps, I adjust the cylinder radius and scale ratio so they sit just outside the lid surface, with a small offset accounting for the scaled geometry. I'm adding rusty iron coloring with an orange-tinted variant for the studs, plus iron end caps at the lid's ends to cover the exposed wood, and planning red velvet for the lid's interior lining.

Now I'm working out the geometry for that velvet lining — a thin flat box sized to match the lid's underside, positioned right at the hinge line. I'm rotating the lid open by -110 degrees and computing how the underside's normal vector transforms, confirming it ends up facing forward and slightly upward so the velvet is visible once opened, with the hinge anchored at the back top edge.

I'm also sketching out the chest body itself: a flat bottom board spanning the full footprint, with front/back/side wall planks stacked up to reach the hinge height, plus a small hasp box attached to the lid front that stays glued to it through the rotation.

Now I'm laying out the plank boards into four stacked rows with slight z-offsets for a relief effect, filling the interior with a dark color, and adding decorative metal strap bands running vertically down the front, back, and sides of the chest at the correct wall thickness.

Adjusting corner bracket sizes slightly, then placing small spherical studs along the metal straps—spacing them every .09 units on front straps and working out positions for studs along the lid's curved arc using ellipse math for the y-coordinates.

Now I'm adding the lock mechanism: an iron staple plate on the front face, a small ring loop for a hanging padlock, and a decorative skull detail near the top of the wood.

Padlock body bottom sits just above the floor. I'm skipping hidden hinge details on the back wall, and setting up shared coin geometry with gold color variants for reuse across coin meshes, using Euler rotations and scattering them across a floor range.

For the coin heap in front of the chest, I'm working out the sphere scale and vertical offset needed so it sits naturally on the floor without clipping below it, settling on a smaller scale and slightly raised center to keep it visually grounded, then placing a trail of spilled coins leading from the chest rim down toward the heap.

Now I'm adding a second gold lump draped over the rim to suggest overflow, then scattering individual heap coins randomly within a disc using a height formula based on the mound's curvature, before positioning gem placements starting with a red gem on the mound.

Continuing with gem placements on the floor and heap, then positioning a goblet resting on the mound surface with its base sunk slightly into the gold, adding small octahedral gems around its cup and a squashed sphere for a stem knob ring.

For the pearl necklace, I'm building a path using catmull-rom interpolation through a set of points, then placing alternating ivory and cream-colored pearl spheres along its length, adding a small gold clasp and a teardrop ruby pendant at the end. I'm deciding to skip rust patches on the straps for now to keep things simpler.

For the materials, I'm defining a mottled rust-brown paint for the iron bands and studs to give them a weathered look, applying it across the lid straps. Then I'm setting up three wood grain paint variants with different tones, orienting the grain axis along x for front/back/lid surfaces and along z for the sides.

Thinking about paint budget, I should bump paint resolution for quality but limit which meshes actually get mottled textures since the chart count adds up fast with ~40 painted meshes. I'll simplify the straps to flat alternating dark tones instead of full mottle to cut down on charts, and note that interior wall faces are mostly hidden by the mound contents anyway so they don't need extra detail.

Checking the mound geometry against the interior walls, I realize the current ellipsoid shape leaves a visible gap at the rim where you can see down into the dark interior — not good. I need a fatter ellipsoid: raising the center and widening the radii so it covers closer to the walls at the rim height, then checking the cross-section at y=.45 to confirm the edge nearly touches the box walls with no visible hole.

I decide instead to fill the interior with a gold box (with a dark gold color) up to a certain height, then place the mound ellipsoid on top of that — this way any small gap at the rim just reveals more gold rather than empty space. Then I move on to positioning the coins scattered across the mound's surface.

For placing objects accurately on the mound, I define a helper function that computes the surface height at any (x,z) position using the ellipsoid equation, so gems, the goblet base, and other scattered items all sit flush against the curved surface rather than floating or clipping. I'll use flat shading on the mound segments for a faceted, gem-like look, and add a small overflow lump of coins spilling slightly over the rim for a natural, overflowing treasure pile appearance.

Building the plank layout...

Now I'm checking the gold fill dimensions against the interior walls to confirm they fit without overlap, and sketching the lid as a half-cylinder shape, working out the rotation needed to orient it correctly over the box.

Adding strap cylinders at the lid ends and end-cap plates, checking scale and offset values against the wood geometry, then starting the velvet lining box.

Now I'm adding the lid tab and slot details, positioning them relative to the lid's front edge so they align with the closed body wall, then setting up the pose rotation for the lid hinge after all lid parts are parented.

For the skull and crossbones decoration, I'm working out the geometry: a flattened sphere for the cranium, a small jaw box, tiny eye sockets, and two crossed bone shapes with knob spheres at each end, calculating the offsets from the rotation angle so everything sits flush against the surface at the right depth.

I'm also positioning the padlock's staple plate relative to the skull, adjusting the vertical placement so the skull's jaw and the plate's top edge overlap correctly without clipping.

Now I'm assembling the padlock itself: a loop torus at the plate's bottom, a small padlock body box, an arched shackle torus, and a dark keyhole indent in brass tones. I'm tilting the whole padlock assembly slightly forward for a more natural hanging pose.

Now I'm plotting the pearl necklace's path through 3D space, computing each point's height above the surface using the top() helper, tracing a curve that dips into the interior and avoids the lid near the back of the treasure chest.

I'll clamp y to stay above the floor since the Catmull-Rom spline can overshoot slightly, then distribute pearl spheres evenly along the path's length using small shared sphere geometry for efficiency.

For the pendant, I'm placing a teardrop-shaped ruby gem with a gold ring at the end of the necklace chain, using an icosahedron geometry scaled to flatten it slightly, with flat shading for a faceted jewel look. I'll add emerald as a second gem color option, plus scattered gold coins and a rim lump near the floor for extra detail.

Now I'm adding hardware for the chest lid: iron hinge boxes at the back of the body and hinge barrel cylinders rotated to sit flush, positioned symmetrically on either side. I'm estimating the overall height of the opened lid and chest, confirming everything clears the floor properly once the lid rotates back.

Now I'm setting up stud placement using a shared sphere geometry, distributing studs along the front and back straps at even y-intervals and working out the curved positions of studs along the lid's arched band using sine-based coordinates.
